::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Prove the function $f(x)$ is discontinuous where $f(x)=1$ for $x>0$ and $f(x)=0$ for $x≤0$ at the point $x = 0$](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2967828/prove-the-function-fx-is-discontinuous-where-fx-1-for-x0-and-fx-0), asked by [Bob](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/607607/bob) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2018-10-23; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I'm stuck on this question and I'm not sure how to approach it. I've been solving a few other proofs with the ε-δ property but I don't think I can apply this here. How would I prove that this is discontinuous at the point x=0?
:::

You want to show that $\lim_{x\to 0} f(x)$ does not exist.

Recall that $\lim_{x\to a} f(x)$ exists if there exists an $L$ such that for every $\epsilon > 0$ there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that for all $x$,
$$0 < |x - a | < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \epsilon.$$
Negating this property requires flipping all the quantifiers down the chain.  We say $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ **does not** exist if *for every* $L$ *there exists* an $\epsilon>0$ such that *for all* $\delta > 0$ *there exists* a point $x$ such that 
$$0 < |x-a| < \delta \text{ and } |f(x) - L| \geq \epsilon.$$

Any $\epsilon$ that separates $L$ from $1$ or $0$ will work.  Given $\delta > 0$, choose a negative $x$ if $L$ is further than $\epsilon$ from $0$, or a positive $x$ if $L$ is further than $\epsilon$ from $1$.
